props.title: Midnight Mary
props.initialSlug: Gangster's moll faces murder trial & dark past

sections.content: **Midnight Mary** (1933) stands as a defining Pre-Code gangster film that pushes boundaries through Loretta Young's revolutionary performance as Mary Martin, a woman forced into crime who refuses to play the typical fallen woman role. Director William Wellman crafts a gritty urban narrative that influenced later film noir, particularly in its use of flashbacks and morally ambiguous protagonists. The film's frank treatment of sexuality and violence would become impossible just one year later with the strict enforcement of the Hays Code, making it a crucial snapshot of Hollywood's brief period of relative creative freedom.

sections.content: Pre-Code Hollywood's treatment of female criminals reached its zenith with films like **Midnight Mary** (1933) and Baby Face (1933), where women weren't simply victims or molls but active participants in the criminal underworld. These films offered unprecedented agency to female characters, allowing them to be as ruthless and complex as their male counterparts. **Ladies They Talk About** (1933) similarly featured Barbara Stanwyck as a bank robber, demonstrating how Pre-Code cinema was uniquely positioned to explore female criminality.

William Wellman's direction in **Midnight Mary** (1933) showcases the visual style that would later define film noir, particularly in its use of shadows and urban nightscapes. This aesthetic approach influenced later classics like **Double Indemnity** (1944) and **The Postman Always Rings Twice** (1946). The film's courtroom framing device, telling its story through flashbacks, was innovative for its time and became a standard technique in crime films. SUBHEAD: Pre-Code Women and Crime

sections.content: The revolutionary aspect of **Midnight Mary** (1933) lies in its refusal to morally condemn its protagonist. Unlike later Code-era films that required criminal characters to face punishment, Mary's story allows for complexity and even sympathy. This approach influenced later femme fatale characters, though they wouldn't enjoy the same moral ambiguity until film noir emerged in the 1940s with works like **Gilda** (1946) and **Out of the Past** (1947).
